title: Thermoregulation and heat dissipation
why_this_matters: Dogs lose heat mainly by panting, not sweating, so heat illness in a working dog develops and responds differently from heat illness in a person.

what_changes_from_human.point: Dogs lose heat mainly by panting and have fewer sweat glands than people, so anything that impairs panting removes their main way to cool.
Cool first, transport second: a dog's temperature can keep rising after exercise stops.
In the studies retrieved, partial water immersion cooled dogs faster than passive cooling or a cooling mat, and faster than alcohol on the paw pads.

takeaway: A dog cools by panting, so protect the airway, start cooling on scene, and do not let a hot dog sit in a hot vehicle.

compare.canine: Panting: evaporation from the upper respiratory tract, with air moved over the nasal and oral surfaces. Dogs have a reduced number of sweat glands compared with humans.
compare.implication: A dog that cannot pant effectively has lost its main cooling route. Upper airway obstruction is a listed risk factor for canine heat stroke.

compare.topic: Where the water for evaporation comes from
compare.canine: The lateral nasal glands are described as supplying a large part of the water for panting and as analogous to sweat glands in man; their evaporation could account for 19 to 36 percent of the increase in respiratory evaporation with thermal panting.
compare.implication: Cooling in dogs is tied to the airway and nose, not the skin surface.

compare.human: Core temperature above about 40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction.
compare.canine: Core temperature above 41 °C with central nervous system dysfunction, in one review.
compare.implication: Do not carry the human threshold over to a dog unchanged. Reviewers to confirm the working definition for the app.

compare.human: Cold-water immersion is a recognised first-line field treatment for exertional heat stroke.
compare.canine: Partial water immersion cooled dogs faster than passive cooling or a cooling mat in one study (time to 39 °C: 16, 36 and 48 minutes). Cold water (0.1 to 15 °C) cooled dogs effectively in a canicross study with no hypothermia or adverse effects seen. Alcohol on the paw pads cooled less efficiently than immersion and raised heart rate more.
compare.implication: Immersion or wet-plus-airflow rather than alcohol on the paw pads. Confirm any limits for a dog that is obtunded.

compare.human: Core temperature generally falls once exertion stops and cooling begins.
compare.canine: In a canicross study, a dog's temperature rose during the first 5 minutes after exercise in 24.4% of cooling profiles, and dogs housed in vehicles cooled less.
compare.implication: Cool first, transport second, and cool the vehicle before loading.
